name: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA peel)
lead: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a strong organic acid that dermatologists apply to the skin as a chemical peel and as a topical agent for destroying warts. As a peel it is used to smooth skin texture, lighten uneven pigment such as sun spots and melasma, and soften some acne and varicella scars; the appearance payoff comes from the skin shedding its damaged outer layers and regrowing.[2][14][15]

The compound was discovered by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839 and is widely used in laboratories to precipitate proteins and nucleic acids.[1] In dermatology a TCA peel is classed as a medium-depth peel, deeper than the light glycolic or salicylic acid peels sold for home use. Wikipedia says medium peels should be performed by a medical provider, usually in a clinic or outpatient surgical setting.[2] A review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology notes that peel depth is directly related to both improved results and the number of complications.[10]

Registered and published studies include TCA peels for acne, melasma, solar lentigines, actinic keratosis and atrophic varicella scars.[4][5][6][7][11][12][13] A point-wise variant known as TCA CROSS is used by clinicians for atrophic scars, but none of the sources cited here describe it.
infobox: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage (ECHA)[1]

paras: TCA is applied to the skin to cause controlled chemical injury, followed by peeling and regrowth. It is regarded as a medium peel, with deeper effects than light superficial acids such as glycolic or salicylic acid.[2][10] Concentration, number of coats and technique influence depth; specific protocols are the province of treating clinicians and are not given here.

Chemical peeling in general goes back to the second half of the nineteenth century, when the Vienna dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra used agents such as phenol and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities, according to Wikipedia.[2] Peels are commonly described in tiers: light peels with alpha or beta hydroxy acids, medium peels with TCA or retinoic acid, and deep phenol-croton oil peels.[2] The JAAC review states that chemical peeling has been used for centuries to improve signs of ultraviolet-induced sun damage and that its scientific basis has developed over the last three decades.[10]

Registered studies have examined TCA for acne vulgaris, melasma, hand lentigines, atrophic varicella scars and acanthosis nigricans.[4][5][6][7][8] Cosmetic uses of TCA also include chemical peels and tattoo removal.[1]

For melasma, a 2024 review in Dermatologic Clinics describes peeling agents including glycolic acid, salicylic acid, TCA, Jessner's solution, retinoic acid and lactic acid as an additional or maintenance therapy for this chronic, recurrent facial pigment disorder.[14] For solar lentigines, a 2025 systematic review of 41 clinical trials covering 3,234 patients compared topical agents, lasers, cryotherapy and chemical peels.[15]

TCA is applied topically to destroy warts, including genital warts, and has been registered in studies for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.[1][9] It has also been reviewed as a treatment option in vitiligo[16] and in actinic keratosis, where a systematic review of 80 randomized trials with 6,748 patients found TCA non-inferior to cryotherapy, imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil, photodynamic therapy and ablative fractional laser in percent clearance.[17]

The European Chemicals Agency classifies TCA as causing severe skin burns and eye damage.[1] Wikipedia lists photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, atrophy and textural change among the complications of deeper peels, and notes injury and scarring from professional and home peels.[2] Patients commonly report a warm or burning sensation during application, and medium peels may be accompanied by oral sedation or local anesthetic.[2]
The IARC lists TCA in Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans), which concerns chemical exposure generally.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a 2022 trial of 25% TCA peel versus 30% salicylic acid peel in mild to moderate acne (n=60)[4], a trial of TCA for atrophic varicella scars (n=100)[5], a melasma trial of modified Jessner's solution with TCA versus glycolic acid with TCA (n=30)[6], a 15% TCA peel for hand lentigines (n=20)[7] and a trial comparing 15% TCA with tretinoin in acanthosis nigricans (n=80).[8] The registry records cited here do not report results, so outcomes are not summarized.

A published trial of 45 Egyptian patients with moderate-to-severe melasma, mostly skin types IV-V, compared 4% hydroquinone cream, 30% TCA peeling and/or Q-switched Nd:YAG laser over about six months using the MASI score. The topically treated group improved significantly more than the other groups (p<0.0001), with no significant difference between laser and peeling; epidermal melasma improved more than dermal.[18] A 2024 trial of 60 melasma patients tested adding systemic metformin to TCA peeling versus TCA alone.[19]
Systematic reviews place TCA among options for actinic keratosis (non-inferior to several other treatments)[17] and chemical peels among treatments for solar lentigines.[15]
TCA peels and TCA CROSS are discussed as clinic procedures in acne-scar and skin-texture conversations. Medical sources describe injury and scarring as risks of both professional and home peels.[2]

timeline.event: Ferdinand von Hebra introduces chemical peels for skin resurfacing in Vienna.[2]
Phenol-croton oil deep peels enter mainstream practice.[2]
A JAAD review sets out key principles for superficial and medium-depth peeling.[10]

card.summary: A medium-depth chemical peel acid used by clinicians for skin texture, pigment and scars; registered trials exist but outcomes aren't reported in the records.
card.note: Caustic acid; burns, pigment change and scarring are possible, so it is described as a provider-performed procedure.

quick.overview:
TCA is a strong acid used as a medium-depth chemical peel and for wart removal. Clinicians use it for texture, pigment and some scars;.

Several small trials are registered for acne, melasma and scars, but the registry entries cited do not report results.
quick.mechanism: The acid causes controlled chemical injury to the skin surface, which then peels and regenerates. Depth depends on concentration and technique.
quick.risks: The European Chemicals Agency says it causes severe skin burns and eye damage. Deeper peels carry risks of prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring, and Wikipedia says medium peels should be done by a medical provider.
